1:
The opening couplet turns on which half is subject and which predicate. Delitzsch calls the case difficult, since such a clause normally puts the predicate first but will front the subject for emphasis; he takes the fronted terms as predicates in both halves, so a man shows he loves knowledge by putting himself in a learner's place, and a man devoid of reason rejects the reproof meant to save him. Ellicott reverses the English outright, rendering it that he who loves knowledge loves discipline, and glosses the brutishness as a blind life within the brain. Clarke keeps the received order but presses the Hebrew for reproof to mean discipline, and reads the word for brutish as bear. Henry makes it a test: we may try whether we have grace by asking how we stand toward the means of grace, and those who take it as an affront to be told their faults are the brutish here meant. Gill widens instruction to the Scriptures, the ministry and the rod of affliction.

On the good man who obtains favour, the readings run from the doctrinal to the plain. Gill insists no man is good naturally and that the favour is drawn out as from a fountain by prayer and repeated acts of faith. Clarke orders it in two steps, God first making the man good, then the man increasing in favour as he obeys. Ellicott fixes the sense from the parallel: the opposite being a man of wicked devices, good here means benevolent. Henry reads a double measure: we are really as we are with God, who judges his children largely by their conduct toward one another.

The root draws them together. Delitzsch finds in the word for wickedness the idea of wanting inward stay, so a life with no support in God can expect no endurance, while the righteous are rooted as trees no storm can tear up. Henry says the same: prosperity raised by sin is built on sand, and though the branches of the righteous may be shaken the root is not moved. Clarke grounds it differently: evil is variable and has no fixed principle, whereas goodness is unchangeable because it comes from God. Gill alone takes it eschatologically, applying the settled state of the wicked to Babylon saying she sits a queen.

The virtuous woman produces the chapter's longest note. Delitzsch renders the phrase a good brave wife, glossing the Hebrew as valour, and sets her beside the pleasant wife praised earlier: that one obtains honour, this one raises her husband to higher honour. Ellicott says the word means of power, of ability and character. Clarke turns it into an essay, deriving the English virtue through man from strength, and arguing that where field labour falls to women physical strength is genuinely the first qualification in a wife; he instances African women going out to the plantations with a mattock and an infant, and takes the verse literally on that ground. On the second half he suspects a specific reference, the woman who makes ashamed bringing actual disease into the bones. Henry keeps the domestic sense and makes the crown both ornament and ensign of power.

The last pair are read as thought and speech in sequence. Delitzsch contrasts the simple plans of the righteous with the worked-out schemes of the godless, the one having an objective rule and the other a selfish purpose. Henry insists we mistake if we imagine thoughts are free: they are under divine cognizance and so under divine command. On the words that lie in wait, Delitzsch takes the sense to be words calculated to bring men into danger of their lives by false charge before a tribunal; Gill applies the whole to the snares laid for Christ and afterwards to the edicts of the beast, while Ellicott and Wesley gloss each half in a line.
7:
The first couplet turns on whether the wicked are overturned or turn about. Delitzsch reports a reading that takes the verb reflexively, so that it is over with them in the turning of a hand; but he decides against it, since the parallel with the house of the righteous makes the wicked the object, and the ancient versions read the verb as overturning. Henry adds the image of the apples of Sodom, which look fair until touched. Clarke keeps it demographic, arguing that the wicked seldom keep many generations in a direct line, and finding in that a mercy, since the entail of iniquity is cut off before the same vices are strengthened by inheritance. Ellicott offers either the judgments of God or the storms that overwhelm a house built on sand.

Praise is then measured out. Delitzsch fixes the Hebrew term as intelligence and nothing else in this book, and insists the praise is proportioned to a man's understanding, which here includes moral discernment; the verb, he adds, means not renown in general but good renown. Ellicott glosses it as knowing the ends to be pursued in life and the means of reaching them, that is, finding out God's will and how to fulfil it. Henry makes it a rule about reputation: the best follows piety and prudent conduct, the worst follows perversity, and Providence will bring the perverse man to contempt.

The proverb about the despised man with a servant is read three ways. Delitzsch reports that many ancients rendered it as being a servant to himself, and answers that the Hebrew would then run differently; keeping the received reading, he takes it as commending the middle rank of life, and quotes the remark that a slave is the first necessity of an oriental in moderate circumstances. Gill records the same alternative without deciding, allowing either the man of small means who keeps a servant or the man who does his own work at home and in the field. Clarke prefers the Latin version outright, that the poor man who provides for himself is better than the proud man destitute of bread, and adds that some would rather starve, through pride of birth, than put their hands to menial labour. Henry keeps it moral: it is folly to covet a great figure abroad while wanting necessaries at home.

The verse about the beast draws the fullest agreement and sharpest writing. Delitzsch will not have it as mere provision, insisting the Hebrew means the creature's state of feeling and the verb a careful investigation acted upon; he gathers the laws giving cattle the sabbath rest and their wages and requiring the dam to be let go, and calls them prefigurations of this knowing. Ellicott renders it more briefly, that the righteous knows their feelings and so can feel for them. Clarke tells how he once found the Hebrew of the clause on an inn sign, which reminded him to feed his horse, then turns the second half into an indictment of horse races, prize fights and wars of ambition. Henry and Wesley both stress that the wicked man's very mercies are cruel, Henry instancing the proposal to chastise Christ and let him go as a pretended kindness covering a purposed cruelty.

The last pair commend work and condemn the shortcut. Delitzsch takes the vain things pursued as things rather than persons, unreal business and windy speculation set against the surest honest support. Ellicott instances searching for hidden treasure. Clarke names field sports and the alehouse, and records a Greek addition about the boon companion at banquets who leaves dishonour in his own strongholds. On the closing verse Delitzsch construes the godless as lusting in vain after the spoil evil-doers take; Gill and Henry note that the same word may be rendered stronghold rather than net, so the wicked man wants a fortress from which to do mischief safely.
13:
Delitzsch marks this as the point where the chapter turns to the tongue. On the snare of the lips he presses a grammatical point: the consecutive form of the second verb makes the escape follow from the first clause rather than stand against it, and he rejects a paraphrase softening the first half into inconsiderate words. Gill offers a second construction, that the snare is laid for others rather than sprung on himself, and applies it to heretics and antichrist. Clarke keeps it homely: a liar has need of a good memory, since having no truth in him he says and unsays and contradicts himself. Ellicott adds the eschatological weight: words are the index of the soul, stored up as witness for the day of judgment. Henry gives the practical version: many a man has felt the lash for want of a bridle on his tongue.

The fruit of the mouth is read as returning to the speaker. Delitzsch takes the fruit as wholesome doctrine and comforting exhortation, so that the blessing bestowed blesses the giver; the Hebrew for what the hands accomplish is double-sided, covering reward and punishment alike, and the proverb finds its final verification at the last judgment. Henry says it in fewer words: while teaching others we may ourselves learn and feed on the bread we break to them. Ellicott adds the bread cast on the waters, returning as love and respect. Gill splits the line differently, allowing that a man may be satisfied by the fruit of another's mouth, a private believer's or a faithful minister's.

On the fool right in his own eyes, Delitzsch draws the distinction: a man's judgment of his own character is confined to a narrow subjectivity, but there are objective criteria by which a way may be tested, and the fool knows no standard but his own opinion, while the wise man is not so wise in his own eyes that he will not hear counsel. Henry turns it: the fool never enquires the way because he is confident he cannot miss it, and he is a fool who is governed by his eye rather than his conscience. Wesley defines the wise man from the other side, as one who distrusts his own judgment and seeks counsel.

The verse on a fool's wrath draws the neatest gloss. Delitzsch quotes a later saying that a man is known by three things, his conduct in drinking, in money, and under deep excitement; the fool shows his vexation the same day while the prudent man hides the dishonour so as not to increase his injury, and passionless retaliation may be a duty of self-preservation where passionate self-defence is always evil. Clarke matches it with the English proverb that a fool's bolt is soon shot. Ellicott gives the covering a positive turn: not ignoring the insult, but waiting to tell the offender of his fault. Henry distinguishes what is covered: the passion in his own breast, since anger is shame, and the provocation given him, which it is a kindness to ourselves to extenuate.

The last two verses set truth against wounding speech. Delitzsch reads the first not as tautology but as a causal connection between a man's character and his utterances, since he who breathes conscientiousness lets the voice of it be heard. Henry commends the faithful witness for showing that he is governed by righteousness, and condemns the false one as possessed by a lying spirit. On the closing verse Delitzsch and Ellicott both correct the English verb to babbling, Delitzsch tracing the Hebrew to speaking at random, Ellicott describing a man who chatters on without noticing how he wounds. Clarke reports a variant in several manuscripts making it a man who trusts in the piercings of a sword, though he judges the received reading right. Henry takes the whole as the tongue being death or life, poison or medicine, as used.
19:
The moment allotted the lying tongue is a real crux. Delitzsch says none of the old translators understood the phrase, and works through the attempts: one takes it as until I split the tongue, which he calls incorrect; another treats the word as a noun with a lengthened ending; a third renders it until I make a moment, which he accepts, the root being the swinging of a balance, so the twinkling of an eye. The cohortative marks a movement freely determined and used to measure time. The others take the sense without the philology. Henry sets the halves against each other: what is true will always be true, while the liar under examination will be found in several stories and inconsistent with himself. Clarke adds that falsehood gains credit only because it was supposed to be truth. Ellicott makes the detection providential; Wesley says liars may make a fair show for a season but are quickly convicted.

The verse on devisers of evil is defended against the charge of saying nothing. Delitzsch admits it looks like a platitude, since a man who forges mischief acts against a neighbour by definition, and answers in two steps: the first half says the evil hatched issues in deceiving that neighbour, and read with the second, that the deceiver at once prepares sorrow for him. He takes the contrasting phrase to mean not those who advise contending parties to make peace, but those who devise peace for a neighbour. Henry and Ellicott both turn the deception back on its author, Henry with the epigram that deceivers will be deceived however artfully they plot, and Ellicott saying they begin by deceiving others and end by deceiving themselves. Gill notes the same root, of ploughing evil and sowing discord.

The promise that no evil befalls the just needs qualifying, and each of them qualifies it differently. Delitzsch fixes the Hebrew as ethical wickedness rather than sorrow, and holds the evil meant to be the harvest of sin, so the godless are full of it because their moral element produces it while nothing of that kind falls on the righteous; God, who gives form to human fortune, remains in the background. Gill splits it into the evil of sin, from which grace preserves, and the evil of punishment, laid on Christ. Henry says both at once, and offers a construction of the whole: no evil happens to the just though the wicked be filled with spite against them. Clarke keeps it short: whatever occurs to a righteous man God turns to his advantage, while the wicked are grieved by every occurrence.

Truth as dealing rather than speech closes the group. Delitzsch defines the Hebrew as probity, the harmony between words and thoughts, and notes that the Greek translators appear to have read a different phrase. Henry draws a double lesson: hate lying, destructive to society as well as a breach of law, and make conscience of truth in actions and not only words. Gill lists what lying contradicts: the nature of God, the Scriptures, the Gospel, the Spirit of truth.

On concealed knowledge they converge, with a difference of motive. Delitzsch notes that this verse repeats an earlier one, the fool who cannot keep his anger matching the heart-fool who trumpets folly; against that charlatan he sets the prudent man who holds his knowledge until the right occasion and hearer, and remarks that though the right motive regulates such silence, the proverb puts it under prudence. Henry adds the tag that the perfection of art is to conceal it, and that the fool either does not wish to hide his folly or cannot. Clarke supplies the blunt version: if a fool holds his peace he may pass for a wise man. Ellicott and Wesley give the pair a line each.
24:
Delitzsch treats these verses as one group, on the means of rising and the two ways that lead to error and to life. On the diligent hand he notes that the second word may be adjective to a hand supplied from the first half or the abstract noun slothfulness, and glosses the last term as tributary service to a master. Henry instances Solomon advancing Jeroboam for industry, and turns the second half on the word's other sense: it is the deceitful, not merely the lazy, who come under tribute. Ellicott supplies the historical picture, the forced labour by which Solomon built. Gill traces the rise from apprentice to master to magistrate; Clarke gives the reason in a line, that the industrious man is independent and so respected.

The verse on heaviness of heart is textually vexed. Delitzsch points out a double anomaly, the noun for trouble construed as masculine and the noun for heart as feminine; the old versions escaped it by supplying a different subject and a later Greek translator read a different verb, but he keeps the text, noting that the other reading loses the rhyme. Clarke names the trouble as sorrow of heart, hopeless love, or a sense of God's displeasure, answered by a single sentence of absolution. Henry makes the good word a promise of God applied by faith. Ellicott turns it into a duty, warning against excessive anxiety and pressing the casting of care on God. Wesley glosses the good word as compassionate or encouraging.

The next verse is the chapter's hardest, and Delitzsch says so: no acceptable meaning comes from the traditional vocalization. He canvasses the ancients, who take the word as a participle meaning surpassing, and those who make the righteous man better or richer in honour; he prefers the reading that it is righteousness and not nobility that raises a man, yet objects that this leaves the two halves isolated, and himself renders it that the righteous looks after his pastures. Clarke reports the same pasture rendering and cannot see how the Hebrew yields it; he lists the Syriac, which makes the righteous devise good for his neighbour, and the Greek, which he calls insufferable for making the righteous his own friend. Ellicott offers both the comparative and the guiding sense, the just man showing his neighbour the way while the wicked wanders. Gill takes the comparison strictly: one righteous man cannot excel another, since all are justified by the same righteousness, so the neighbour meant must be unrighteous.

The slothful hunter is contested at the verb. Delitzsch reports that four ancient versions render it as catching, and objects that the stem nowhere means that; the Jewish lexicographers all arrive at singeing or roasting, which yields either that the man is too lazy to hunt or that having his prey he does not prepare it. Ellicott takes the netting sense without argument. Clarke finds real obscurity here, and concludes that the received text is best if the first word is taken as fraudulent rather than slothful, justice snatching from the man's mouth what he got unrighteously. Gill offers the fowler's practice of burning captured birds' wing feathers as background.

The closing verse turns on a single vowel. Delitzsch observes that all the old versions read the last word as the preposition to rather than the negative, and so had to extract a sense about a devious way leading to death; he answers that the noun means a step and not a devious way, that the two words are distinguished by their vowels in the Babylonian pointing, and that the received text stands, giving immortality. Henry reads the way as a highway cast up by God, with life in it and not only at its end. Clarke makes it practical: every duty and act of faith leads to life, since the path of duty is the way of safety.
